earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern

earlier_scan.note: Fixed initial primary stress; secondary on odd syllables (3rd, 5th, 7th)

new_statements.quote: Arabana-Wangkangurru follows the majority of Australian languages in having a strong stress accent on the first syllable of a word. There are no monosyllabics (except for Eastern Wangkangurru ko 'yes'); in words of two or three syllables there is simply the one accent falling on the first syllable. [...] As described by Dixon (1980a:138) for other Australian languages, longer words have a secondary stress on the third, fifth and seventh syllable, the secondary accent being marked here by a grave accent [...] In long words consisting of several morphemes another rule supersedes this: each bound morpheme of two or three syllables has a secondary accent on its first syllable.
new_statements.citation: Hercus, Luise A. 1994. A Grammar of the Arabana-Wangkangurru Language, Lake Eyre Basin, South Australia. Pacific Linguistics C-128. Canberra: ANU.
new_statements.locator: §2.12 Accentuation, pp. 47-48 (pp. 67-68 of the archive.org scan)

There are no monosyllabics (except for Eastern Wangkangurru ko 'yes'); in words of two or three syllables there is simply the one accent falling on the first syllable. This is in contr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of every word. Words of two or three syllables carry only that one accent. Longer monomorphemic words add secondary stress on the 3rd, 5th, 7th syllables (left-to-right alternation from the initial); in long polymorphemic words the morphological rule overrides the alternating count: each bound morpheme of two or three syllables takes a secondary accent on its own first syllable (e.g. kátha-nàngka-lìparna).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: on 3rd, 5th, 7th syllables of long words (káthartìngka 'corella', Yúrkunàngku); superseded in polymorphemic words by a secondary accent on the first syllable of each 2-3-syllable bound morpheme (kúdna-tyúrra-àpu-kànha, kátha-rnda-nángka-lìparna, thárni-la-mìntya-nàngka-ngura). Enclitics -malaru / manarni have no first-syllable accent and a secondary accent on their second syllable (p. 259).
new_statements.exceptions: Two: (1) exclamations, vocatives and imperatives that are shouted with distortion of the final syllables always carry the main accent on the final syllable (Ánari yùkarndéi! 'Come here!', Yàkayéi! 'Oh dear!', cf. §2.13.2(3)); (2) song, where any syllable, especially the final one, can be stressed. Only monosyllable is the loan ko 'yes' (Eastern Wangkangurru). Loans from Aranda follow the Wangkangurru (initial) system rather than the Arandic first-consonant-initial-syllable rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in ordinary speech, stated for the combined Arabana-Wangkangurru language (both dialects); examples are citation/text forms. The chapter is a phonology chapter of a reference grammar based on fieldwork with the last fluent speakers (chiefly Wangkangurru speaker Mick McLean Irinyili).
new_statements.identity_note: Hercus 1994 treats Arabana and Wangkangurru as two dialects of one language, 'Arabana-Wangkangurru', and states the accentuation rule for the combined language (Glottolog splits them: Arabana = arab1267, Wangganguru = wang1290, with dialects Eastern Wangganguru east2873, Marlu-papu-nganha marl1234, Mikiri-nganha miki1244). The statement explicitly names the Wangkangurru system ('Words borrowed from Aranda follow the Wangkangurru system') and the main consultant was Wangkangurru speaker Mick McLean Irinyili, so it applies to wang1290; the same statement can serve arab1267, where Harvey et al. 2019 independently report initial primary stress plus secondary stress.

Syllables with secondary stress are phonetically, but not psycholinguistically, strong'; pre-stopping is principally found in primary-stressed syllables.

tone.quote: Most Wangkangurru words carry the stress on the first syllable of the word. The 'stressed' part of the word is in bold in these examples: kapirri goanna / mayarru rat / padni no [...] ko 'yes' and padni 'no' questions are easy to ask in Wangkangurru. Simply raise your voice at the end of the sentence to make a questioning tone, as you would in English.
tone.locator: Pronunciation guide, 'More tips on pronunciation', p. 14; 'Questions', p. 31
